newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CHELSEA PROMISE GREATER THINGS TO COME.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CHELSEA PROMISE GREATER THINGS TO COME.

text.p: Chelsea's manager Ruud Gullit, who has won more than his fair share of honours in a distinguished playing career, said he was sure the club would go on to greater things after their F.A. Cup victory on Saturday.
"We are going to do better," said Gullit, who captained the Netherlands to European Championship glory and won European Cup winners' medals with AC Milan.

"We are on the road now and getting better all the time," said Gullit who dedicated the victory to Matthew Harding, Chelsea's 42-year-old vice chairman who was killed in a helicopter crash last October.
"I think spiritually he was with us today and I think all the players wanted to win it for him and for his memory," he added.
Gullit continued: "We played pefectly today. It was hot and humid and difficult for the players to give 90 minutes total football. But we did not give much away and our defence today was perfect.
"All year we have played good football but not always with discipline. Today we were disciplined."
Gullit, who has often expressed surprise at the importance the English gave to the Cup said he could now tell people what it felt like to win it. "I am very proud," he said.
"Lots of people told me I did not realise what it meant for Chelsea fans to win a trophy after 26 years -- they are right -- but I am very happy for the fans now," he said.
Chelsea, a team that traditionally promise much and provide little for their fans, last won the F.A. Cup in 1970 and followed it up with the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1971.
Gullit said his foreign signings had enhanced the side and both the home-grown and imported players had benefitted.
"The English players were keen to learn skills from the foreigners and the English taught the foreigners a new appraoch," he said.
Gianfranco Zola, who scored for Italy against England the last time he played at Wembley, said the stadium was "a special, special place".
"This is one of the best moments of my career. Every player wants to live a moment like I am living now," said Zola, who has just been named England's Footballer of the Year.
Roberto Di Matteo said the goal he scored after 43 seconds -- the fastest strike since the final moved to Wembley in 1923 -- even took him by surprise.
"I took the ball to 25 metres and thought why shouldn't I try a shot. I was so confused I didn't realise I'd scored."
Middlesbrough's Brazilian midfielder Juninho said the early goal had been a severe blow and they never really recovered.
It capped a season he described as "my worst in club football" with relegation and the loss of two cup finals plus recent news he had been dropped from the Brazil side for a tournament in France.
It was widely expected that he played his last match for Middlesbrough -- as did his fellow Brazilian Emerson, Italian Fabrizio Ravanelli and possibly Gianluca Festa.
Middlesbrough Manager Bryan Robson said he was trying to think positively despite his disappointment.
"It is a major achievement reaching two cup finals especially for a club like Middlesbrough who had never got to a major final," he said.

"I feel the club is going in the right direction. My job is to pick everyone up. We'll talk over the summer to the players and make decisions about how to get us back into the premier league," he added.
Chelsea will now represent England in the European Cup Winners' Cup next season and meet Manchester United in the pre-season curtain-raiser Charity Shield at Wembley in August.
French defender Franck Leboeuf said: "When I warmed up before the match I started to cry a bit because I could not believe the fans and the atmosphere.
"They were tremendous. We have to keep this atmosphere. We have to win the Cup Winners' Cup and maybe the championship."
